difficultyReason: The argument turns on a methodological assumption buried inside the study design: that reduced biomarker levels reliably proxy for reduced disease incidence. The correct weakener attacks this hidden link rather than the overt causal claim. Distractors include a strengthener, a choice that attacks a trivial premise, an irrelevant epidemiological fact, and a choice that weakens only a neighboring claim without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical company conducted a four-year clinical trial in which patients with early-stage arterial inflammation were given a daily dose of Verathin. At the trial's end, participants' blood levels of C-reactive protein—a standard biomarker for arterial inflammation—had declined by an average of 34 percent compared with baseline. The company concluded that Verathin reduces the risk of developing full arterial disease in patients with early-stage inflammation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the company's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated C-reactive protein levels frequently return to baseline within four years even in patients who receive no treatment for arterial inflammation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who maintain low C-reactive protein levels over extended periods are significantly less likely to develop full arterial disease than those whose levels remain elevated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The trial participants were recruited from a single hospital network and may not be representative of all patients with early-stage arterial inflammation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some participants in the trial reported mild gastrointestinal side effects during the first month of Verathin use, but these effects resolved without intervention.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several other drugs approved for arterial inflammation also produce measurable reductions in C-reactive protein levels.

explanations.correct: The argument's hidden load-bearing assumption is that the observed decline in C-reactive protein levels was caused by Verathin rather than by natural disease progression. Choice A reveals that CRP levels often drop by themselves over the same time horizon even without treatment—a classic alternative explanation that severs the causal link between Verathin and the biomarker reduction, thereby undermining the conclusion that Verathin reduces disease risk.
explanations.A: Correct. This introduces a rival causal explanation (spontaneous regression) for the observed CRP decline, directly attacking the premise-to-conclusion move that Verathin drove the improvement and therefore reduces disease risk.
explanations.B: This is an opposite-answer trap. It actually strengthens the argument by confirming that low CRP levels—the very outcome Verathin produced—are associated with lower disease incidence, bolstering the company's conclusion.
explanations.C: This attacks the external validity of the sample, which is a legitimate methodological concern, but it only weakens the generalizability of the findings rather than the core causal conclusion about Verathin's effect in the patients who were studied. The conclusion is about patients with early-stage inflammation broadly, but the narrow-sample point does not show Verathin failed to reduce CRP or disease risk—it is a 'too narrow' distractor.
explanations.D: This is an accurate-but-irrelevant distractor. Transient gastrointestinal side effects that resolved spontaneously have no bearing on whether Verathin reduces the risk of developing full arterial disease.
explanations.E: This is a shift-in-subject trap. The fact that other drugs also lower CRP does not undermine the claim that Verathin lowers CRP and thereby reduces disease risk; it merely establishes that Verathin is not unique in this effect, which is irrelevant to the truth of the company's conclusion.
